nameStory: The Branched Sapsucker gets its name from its tree-like, branching body extensions called cerata that look like tiny branches reaching out from its back. These 'branches' help it blend in with the green algae it feeds on, while the 'sapsucker' part refers to how it literally sucks the cell contents from algae like a tiny plant vampire!
description: This is a tiny sea slug about the size of a pencil eraser that lives in New England's tidal pools and shallow coastal waters. Its most striking feature is its collection of finger-like projections that branch out from its back, giving it an almost plant-like appearance. Despite looking somewhat like the colorful nudibranchs you might see in tide pools, it's actually a different type of sea slug called a sacoglossan. Its body is typically translucent green due to the algae cells it steals and stores in its tissues.

idTips.label: Branched projections
idTips.description: Look for multiple finger-like extensions branching from the back that feel soft and squishy when gently touched underwater, resembling tiny green tree branches

idTips.label: Translucent green color
idTips.description: The body appears semi-transparent with a greenish tint, especially visible when backlit, caused by stored algae chloroplasts inside its tissues

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically smaller than your thumbnail, requiring close inspection to see clearly, often mistaken for a piece of algae until it moves

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a slow, steady gliding motion across surfaces rather than the undulating swimming of some other sea slugs

idTips.label: Habitat association
idTips.description: Almost always found directly on or very near green filamentous algae, which feels slippery and thread-like to the touch

habitat: Look for Branched Sapsuckers in New England's rocky tide pools, shallow bays, and protected coastal areas from Maine to Connecticut. They're typically found crawling on green algae growing on rocks, pier pilings, or in eelgrass beds in the intertidal and shallow subtidal zones. The best spots are sheltered areas with good water circulation where filamentous green algae thrive.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures rise and algae begins its spring growth, making this a good time to spot them on fresh green algae in tide pools.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time when both the slugs and their algae food are most abundant and visible in warm, well-lit shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still present but may be less noticeable as algae growth slows and water temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, though they may still be found in deeper tide pools or slightly offshore where temperatures remain more stable.

funFact: This little sea slug is basically a solar-powered animal! It steals chloroplasts (the green parts that make plants photosynthesize) from the algae it eats and keeps them alive in its body tissues, allowing it to supplement its diet with energy from sunlight just like a plant.
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for nudibranchs due to their similar branched appearance, but nudibranchs typically have more colorful, elaborate projections and don't have the distinctive green coloration. Memory trick: if it's green and on green algae, it's likely a Branched Sapsucker!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sapsucker,' this sea slug is completely unrelated to the sapsucker birds that drill holes in trees. The name confusion comes from both organisms' habit of extracting liquid nutrients from their food sources, but one lives in trees while the other lives in tide pools.
compareHints: As the only Placida species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other small sacoglossan sea slugs in the family Limapontiidae. Unlike its relatives that may have simple, unbranched projections, the Branched Sapsucker's distinctive tree-like branching pattern makes it relatively easy to identify. Other family members typically lack the pronounced branching and may appear more worm-like or have fewer, simpler projections.
